what_is_quest.title: What Quest is
what_is_quest.text:
Quest helps you set a transformative goal and reach it. You describe what you want, Quest turns it into an evidence-backed plan, and then you track it, reflect on it, and adjust it over time. You can do all of this alone, or bring in an AI assistant, a mentor, a team, or a community.

## What you can do with it

You do not have to use all of this. Pick what helps.

- **Plan from evidence.** Run a [Deep Inquiry](/guide/deep-inquiries) to research your goal across the [perspectives](/guide/perspectives) you choose, then accept the strategies you want.
- **Test what works for you.** Run small [experiments](/guide/experiments#experiments-in-plain-words) on your own life and let Quest read what your record shows.
- **Run a plan day to day.** Your [plan](/guide/quests-and-plans) becomes milestones, dated goals, and recurring habits on a Today view and a Schedule.
- **Talk to [Quest AI](/guide/quest-ai).** Ask it to adjust a plan, add a goal, or do work for you.
- **Reflect.** A short [daily reflection and period reviews](/guide/productivity) keep you on pace.
- **Track anything** with free [Data Collections](/data-collections/).
- **Bring people in.** Get a [mentor](/guide/mentors), share quests with a [team](/guide/teams), or join [communities](/guide/communities).

plans_free.title: Plans and pricing: the Free plan
plans_free.text:
## Free

The Free plan is genuinely useful on its own. This is the written record of what free users get, and the same list appears on the billing screen and the public pricing page. Check each line against the product before you change it.

- **Up to 1,000 quests that you plan yourself.** These are quick quests: you build the goals and habits.
- **Daily reflection and period reviews** for week, month, quarter, and year.
- **Data Collections and notes** for your own data, with full export.
- **Quest's communities.** Join planets and towns and invite anyone.
- **Quest AI chat for how Quest works.** It answers questions about the app. On Free it cannot read or change your quests.
- **Web and mobile apps.**
- **A free 31 day trial of Quest AI.**

The Free plan does not include AI-assisted quest creation, Quest AI chat that works on your quests, AI tasks, AI plan generation, Deep Inquiries and scientific analysis of your goals, or AI insights in your reflections and reviews (the daily reflection and period reviews themselves stay free, and so does what you already saved). When you reach for one of those, Quest invites you to start the trial or subscribe.

plans_trial.title: Plans and pricing: the 31 day trial
plans_trial.text:
## The 31 day trial

When you create your account, a **31 day free trial of Quest AI** begins. During the trial you get the full Quest AI experience: AI-assisted quest creation up to 1,000 quests, AI plan generation, up to 50 Deep Inquiries a day, Quest AI chat, AI tasks, and AI insights in your reflections and reviews.

When the trial ends, you keep everything you made. You move to the Free plan unless you subscribe.

plans_quest_ai.title: Plans and pricing: Quest AI
plans_quest_ai.text:
## Quest AI

**$10 per month, or $100 per year.** Everything in the trial, ongoing:

- AI-assisted quest creation, up to 1,000 quests.
- Up to 50 Deep Inquiries per day. A Deep Inquiry looks at your goal from several expert perspectives and draws on research and people's real experiences, then uses what it finds to suggest strategies that fit you. It takes a few minutes.
- Quest AI chat with the ability to act on your quests, and AI tasks that run delegated work.
- AI plan generation: strategies and goals written for a quest.
- AI insights in daily reflections and period reviews, including the written proposals for suggested changes to your plan. See [Insights](/guide/insights#plans).

share_howto.title: How-to: share one goal
share_howto.text:
## I want to share one goal with my partner or coach, but keep the rest private

Invite them to **that single quest** by email. Your other quests stay private. For a group that owns goals together, use a [team](/guide/teams) instead. See [Sharing a quest](/guide/quests-and-plans#sharing-a-quest).

share_guide.title: Quests and plans: sharing a quest
share_guide.text:
## Sharing a quest

Quests are private to you by default. When you want help on one, you have two options.

- **Share with a person.** Invite someone by email to a single quest. Your other quests stay private. This is good for a friend, partner, or accountability buddy. If they already have a Quest account, they also get a notification (push and in-app) about the invitation, in addition to the email, so they do not have to be watching their inbox to notice it.
- **Share with a team.** Put a quest on a team's shelf so a whole group owns and moves it together, with roles and assignments. On the quest's dashboard, tap **More**, then **Share with a team** (shown when you are on at least one team), or add it from the team page. See [Teams](/guide/teams).

habit_howto.title: How-to: add a recurring action
habit_howto.text:
## I want to add a recurring action, like meditate every morning

Add a **habit**. Give it a schedule (for example, every weekday morning) and it will appear on **Today** and **Schedule**. Log it each time as done, partial, or not. See [Habits](/guide/quests-and-plans#habits).

calendar_howto.title: How-to: Quest and your calendar
calendar_howto.text:
## I want Quest to know about my real calendar

Go to **Settings > Calendar Sync** and connect Google Calendar or a calendar from your phone. Under **Calendar to Quest**, turn on "Show events on Quest and use for AI scheduling" so your events appear in Quest as goals and inform your Schedule and the AI's scheduling suggestions, and under **Quest to Calendar** turn on "Add Quest schedule to this calendar" if you also want your goals and habits written out to it. See [Calendar Sync](/guide/calendar-sync).

quest_ai_recording.title: Quest AI: recording things as you go
quest_ai_recording.text:
### Recording things as you go

You can record your day straight into a quest from chat, in a sentence:

- "Mark my morning run habit done for today." It shows as done on Today's Actions, the same as tapping Done.
- "I stretched for 15 minutes, log that against my stretching habit." The minutes count toward the habit's daily target. Under the target it shows as started, at or over it as done.

first_quest_intro.title: Create your first quest: before you start
first_quest_intro.text:
# Create your first quest

This walkthrough takes you through creating an AI-assisted quest from start to finish. The first screen says it takes about 10 minutes; plan 15 to 20 if you want to write each part carefully. You can leave and come back; your progress is saved as you go.

A quest is a big goal or an intent: something you would still be working toward in a month or a year. It is the specification of one intention plus the plan that carries it out, not a checklist, so tasks with no outcome behind them belong in your goals and habits.

## Quick quest or AI-assisted quest

Quest starts on a screen titled **Begin Your Quest**. You write what you want to achieve (your vision statement), and then choose:

- **Continue** starts the AI-assisted quest described on this page: five steps, with research and a plan built with you.
- **Continue without AI** makes a **quick quest**. A **Quick Quest Setup** window asks for your vision again (you can edit it), and **How long will this take?**, which you answer either as a **Duration** (a number of Days, Weeks, Months or Years) or as an **End Date**. Tap **Create Quest**. You then build the goals and habits yourself from the quest page. A quick quest uses the same plan structure but skips the research steps and the full specification, and it needs no AI.

What each plan includes (exact numbers in [Plans and pricing](/reference/plans)):

- **Free plan:** quick quests, up to 1,000. AI-assisted creation is not included. If you tap **Continue** without it, Quest invites you to subscribe to Quest AI, and, if you have never used AI-assisted creation, offers **Try it once, free**, which builds one quest and its plan.
- **31 day trial and paid plans (Quest AI, Quest Guided):** AI-assisted creation, up to 1,000 quests.

Both kinds make the same sort of plan, so you can start quick and add AI later, or the reverse.

first_quest_context.title: Create your first quest: step 2, context
first_quest_context.text:
### Measurable outcomes (Metrics)

*How will you know it is real?* These become the Metrics that show your vision is real. Check your vision, write why it matters, then list your measurable outcomes: one per line, each with its number or threshold, such as "I run 60 km a week". Tap **Get AI suggestions** to have Quest score your vision and outcomes and propose better ones, then **Use these outcomes** to take them. When you started from a spec and have no outcomes yet, the lines start from the spec's most common metrics, adapted to you.

On **Continue**, each line is saved as a measurable outcome. Quest reads the target number and unit from your wording (60 and km in the example) and never adds one you did not write. A line that matches an outcome you already have keeps its progress. If the targets cannot be read, your outcomes are still saved, without numbers.

### Current state (Problems)

*Where are you now, and what have you tried?* Next, the AI turns this into the Problems your strategies address. Tell Quest where you are starting from: what is in the way, what you have already tried and how it went, and facts with numbers and dates where you have them. As you write, Quest may ask follow-up questions; tap **Ask more questions** for another round.

### Preferences (Ideals)

*What principles must your strategies honor, and what will you not do?* These become the Ideals every strategy must honor: the values, tradition, limits and qualities every strategy has to respect, plus the approaches and tools you favor or refuse, such as "no medication" or "30 minutes each morning".

core_quest.title: Core concepts: quest and its two ways to make one
core_quest.text:
## Quest

A **quest** is the specification of one intention of yours, plus the plan that carries it out. The specification says where you want to end up (the outcome), why it matters (the purpose), where you stand now and what you have tried (the current state), how you will know you arrived (the acceptance criteria), and what you prefer. Around it sit your plan, progress, reflections, and any people or AI helping you. A quest is not a checklist, and most things in the app hang off a quest.

You can have many quests at once. Each quest lives in a life category (a [planet](#planets-towns-and-the-galaxy)) such as Health, Relationships, or Spirituality.

There are two ways to make one:

- **Quick quest:** a lightweight quest: you write the outcome and plan yourself, without the full specification. Always free, no AI required.
- **AI-assisted quest:** Quest interviews you, can run a Deep Inquiry, and builds the plan with you, in five steps: Vision, Context, Grounded Strategies, Experiments, Plan. Included in the 31 day trial and paid plans (on Free you can try it once). It asks for detail on purpose: see [why creating a quest is so detailed](/getting-started/your-first-quest#why-creating-a-quest-is-so-detailed).

reflection.title: Productivity workflow: daily reflection
reflection.text:
## Daily reflection

The daily reflection is a short check-in that bookends your day. In one sitting you look back at how the last day went, then write the plan for the next one in plain words. It reads top to bottom as one train of thought in two parts: **what happened**, then **what's next**. Each part sits in its own colored box, and tapping a part's heading folds it away so you can focus on the other. Every field is optional, so a reflection can be two sentences or a full page.

The daily reflection is part of every plan, including Free. The AI-written pieces inside it (suggestions drawn from your insights) are covered under [Daily reflection on the Free plan](#daily-reflection-on-the-free-plan).

### Choose Today or Tomorrow

Under the title, a **Today / Tomorrow** switch sets which day you are reviewing and planning for.

- **Today**: look back at **yesterday**, then plan **today**. This is the morning version. The questions read "How did yesterday go?" and "What's your plan for today?"
- **Tomorrow**: look back at **today**, then plan **tomorrow**. This is the evening version. The questions read "How did today go?" and "What's your plan for tomorrow?"

The reflection opens on **Today** before 6 PM and on **Tomorrow** from 6 PM on, and you can switch at any time. Each day keeps its own reflection and plan.

- **What's your plan?** Describe the day in plain words, with times if you have them ("Meditate at 7am, work on the proposal 9 to 12, call Mom at 2pm"). On the next screen Quest turns it into individual goals for you to check.

### What the daily reflection does for your progress

A short daily reflection keeps the week from drifting. It puts a few minutes of looking back and deciding what is next at the edge of every day, so the plan you made for a quest meets the day you are actually having.

What it does in practice:

- **It keeps your schedule honest.** Yesterday's unfinished goals are in front of you, with a **Today** button to move each to today or a calendar button to pick another day.
- **It turns intention into a timed day.** You write the day in your own words, and Quest turns it into individual goals under the right quests, with times, ready to check off on **Today**.
- **It gets the plan out of your head.** Quest's science page cites research that writing a concrete plan for an unfinished task freed the attention the task had been quietly using. Writing the day's plan is that step, taken daily.
- **It builds a record.** What you write is saved, and the passages you confirm are attached to the quests they concern. Your [period reviews](#period-reviews), your [insights](/guide/insights) and your AI read that record, so a review starts from what happened and not from memory.
- **It ties the day to the quest.** Each goal you keep belongs to a quest, so the day's work moves the larger intention it came from.

**What is the point of a daily reflection?** To keep each day connected to your quests. You look back (what got done, what did not, what you learned), then decide what the next day holds, so unfinished work is moved on purpose and what you learned is kept.

**How long does it take?** It is short by design, and every field is optional. You can write a line in each box, or only the plan, and tap **Continue**. Speaking it with the mic is faster than typing.

period_reviews.title: Productivity workflow: period reviews
period_reviews.text:
A period review is a longer reflection for a **week, month, quarter, or year**. It is the daily reflection's larger sibling: you look back over the whole period, deal with what you did not finish, and set up the next one, with the AI doing the sorting and you making each decision.

Open the **Today** tab. Under **Review & Planning** there is a button for each period: **Weekly** (7 days), **Monthly** (30 days), **Quarterly** (3 months) and **Yearly** (12 months). Tap one to start that review.

### What a period review does for you

- See your stats and what you completed in the period, including how your time was spread across the areas of your life.
- Reflect on how it went and say what you want to focus on next.
- Have the AI take into account the notes you saved on your quests during the period, each labeled with where it came from (for example your daily reflection) and its date. It reads those notes, never the reflection text itself.
- Go through what you did not finish and choose, per goal, whether to move it forward, keep it, or abandon it.
- Get suggested goals for the next period, and accept the ones you want straight into your plan.

Nothing changes in your plan until you choose it. Moving or abandoning a goal is applied when you tap **Next** on the **Backlog** step, goals you confirm are added when you continue, and suggestions are added only when you tick them and finish with **Review Complete!**.

### Trajectory

For **measurable goals**, the **Statistics** step of a period review shows a **Goal Trajectory**: it compares your logged data against each goal's target and marks it **Ahead**, **On pace**, **At risk** or **Done**, with a progress bar. This turns a vague "am I doing okay?" into a clear read on pace, early enough to adjust. Set a target number on a goal to get this (see [Goals](/guide/quests-and-plans#goals)). A goal at risk can also trigger a [suggested change to your plan](#suggested-changes-to-your-plan).

**Do reviews change my plan automatically?** No. You decide each move, abandon and accepted suggestion. Quest suggests changes to your plan from your own data, but never applies one until you accept it, and you can **Undo** it. See [Suggested changes to your plan](#suggested-changes-to-your-plan).

collections.title: Data Collections: what they are and how they differ from habits
collections.text:
# Data Collections

Data Collections are Quest's flexible logs for any recurring data: dreams, journals, workouts, moods, practice sessions, symptoms, anything you want to track over time. You define the fields, add entries, and export everything whenever you like.

Collections are **free for everyone**, on every plan, with or without an active quest. If all you want is a good dream journal, Quest is as simple as a dedicated app. When you need more, the same tool scales to detailed, structured tracking.

## What a collection is

A collection has a name, an icon and color, and a set of **fields** that define what each entry records. Add entries over time, and each one captures the fields you defined plus the date. You can tag entries, search them, and filter them.

Its purpose is to keep a record of anything you want to look back on, in the shape you choose, without a schedule or a score attached. The record belongs to you: you can export it at any time, and if you link it to a quest, Quest and your [Deep Inquiries](/guide/deep-inquiries) can use it as real material about your life.

## Collections, habits and Insights

Three things in Quest are stored as collections, and they do different jobs:

- **A collection** is a log you add to whenever you like. It has no schedule, no reminders and no place on Today, and logging to it does not earn wisdom points.
- **A habit** is a recurring action with a schedule and a target. It appears on Today and Schedule, can remind you, earns wisdom points and counts toward your quest's progress. Under the hood it is a collection of type Habit, which is why you can add your own fields to a habit entry. See [Habits and custom tracking](/guide/habits).
- **Insights** is one particular collection that Quest creates for you, built for quick capture of a thought by typing or voice. Quest links each insight to your quests and brings the ones you have not acted on back in your daily reflection and period reviews. See [Insights](/guide/insights).

A collection you make yourself can do none of that on its own. Choose a collection for a dream journal, a symptom log or a practice record. Choose a habit for something you want to do on a schedule and be reminded about.

## Who collections suit

- People who want a simple journal or log with no quest at all, such as a dream journal.
- People tracking something specific to their practice or health, where the fields matter (a lucidity rating, a technique, a duration).
- People who want their own data in a spreadsheet-friendly form, with full export.
- People who want a quest's AI to see real patterns from their life, by linking a collection to that quest.

## Exporting your data

Your data is yours, and you can take it out at any time in the format you need:

- **CSV** for spreadsheets.
- **JSON** for complete, structured data with all fields.
- **TXT** for plain, readable text.
- **PDF** for a printable copy.

**On the web** the file downloads to your browser's download folder. **On the phone app (Android and iOS)** Quest creates the file and opens your phone's share sheet, where you choose what to do with it: save it to Files or Google Drive, send it in a message or email, or open it in another app. Quest only says the export is complete once the file has been handed over. If you close the share sheet without choosing, nothing is saved and you can export again. If Quest cannot create or open the file, it tells you why and offers **Try again**.

You can export one collection from its export button, or several at once from the collections list.

## Collections and quests

Collections can stand alone, or feed your quests:

- **Link a collection to a quest** so the data you log there is part of that quest's context. Open the collection's settings, find **Linked Quests**, and search your quests by name to link one. You never need a quest id.
- A habit you track is itself a small collection under the hood, which is why habit entries can carry rich custom fields.

Linking is optional. Many people keep a journal or dream log with no quest attached at all. When you do link one, the patterns in your data give Quest and your [Deep Inquiries](/guide/deep-inquiries) real material to personalize your plan.

A collection can also drive a measurable outcome. A metric can be calculated from one of your collections or habits (a total, an average, a count, the latest value, the share of entries that meet a rule, or a streak of days), so the outcome moves as you log. See [Productivity workflow](/guide/productivity#period-reviews).

habit_tracking_types.title: Habits and custom tracking: the four types
habit_tracking_types.text:
## Habit types

When you add a habit you answer one question, **What do you want to track?**, and choose one of four types. All four can repeat on any schedule, carry custom fields, and have reminders and alarms.

### Simple Check-In

Mark the habit **Complete**, **Partial** or **Skip** each time. Choose it when doing the habit is a yes or no, or when a half-done day should still be recorded. Examples: morning meditation, take vitamins, make the bed.

### Frequency-Based

Complete the habit a set number of times per period: "Complete [3] times per [week]". The period (day, week, month, quarter or year) comes from the Frequency you picked. Each time you do it, you log one session. Choose it when how often matters more than how long. Examples: exercise three times a week, call a parent twice a month, floss twice a day.

### Quantity

Track an amount against a target. You set a **Target Amount** and a **Unit** (for example 30 pages, 5 miles, 8 glasses of water), and each time you log, you enter how much you did. Today shows your progress as "achieved / target unit". Choose it when the number is the point. Examples: read 30 pages, run 5 miles.

### Timer

Track time on a clock. Choose **Stopwatch** (counts up) or **Countdown** (counts down from your **Target Time**, set in minutes and seconds). Press play on the habit in Today or Schedule and Quest counts the session. Choose it when time spent is the measure. Examples: meditate 20 minutes, practice piano 45 minutes, study 2 hours a day. A running timer belongs to your account, not to one device, so you can start it on your phone and stop it from your laptop, and the time is logged once. See [Tracking types](/guide/quests-and-plans#tracking-types).

life_design.title: Life design
life_design.text:
# Life design

## What life design is

Life design is a short set of questions that helps you name what you are living for, then gives your quests somewhere to sit. You answer once, in about five minutes, and you can come back to your answers whenever you like. In the app it is called **Life Design**.

Your answers become a few **top intents**: short statements of what you want your life to be about, such as "A body that carries me" or "Work that matters". Each quest then belongs to one intent, and your quest list groups them that way. An intent has a name and a vision statement (what the intent looks like once it is real, written as already true).

It is optional. If you never start it, your quest list works exactly as it always has.

## Why it exists

A long list of quests tells you what you are doing, not why. Life design adds one level above your quests, so the why is written down and the quests sit under it.

Quest's own words for it, as you see them in the app:

- Before you begin: "Your answers in the next five minutes may change how you see yourself for the rest of your life."
- "If you follow through on your quests, you will be permanently transformed. You may also transform the world around you."
- "Quest is for big, transformative goals you work on for months or years. It's also for managing everything in your life, to keep you focused on those goals."
- On the first quest step: "A quest is a big goal with a planned completion date. All of your habits, daily tasks, and milestones will live underneath a quest. This way you know that everything you do today is aligned with your highest life intentions."
- On the invitation card: "Five minutes to name what you are living for. Your quests will sit under it."

In practice: the questions run from the end of your life, to everything you want and must do, to a handful of intentions at the top. Starting from the end means the ordinary pressure of your to-do list does not decide what matters. Your quests, habits and daily tasks then line up under intents you chose.

## Who it suits

- Someone with many quests, habits and obligations who feels busy but unsure it adds up to the life they want.
- Someone just starting, who has no big goal yet. Life design ends by helping you pick one (see "When you sign up" below).
- Someone whose work and personal life pull in different directions, and who wants each quest filed under the part of life it serves.
- A team or organization that wants shared intents its members' quests can sit under (see "Organization and team intents" below).

It is less useful if you want a flat list and nothing more. Then skip it: nothing else in Quest depends on it.

**Is life design required?** No. It is optional, and nothing else in Quest depends on it. People who already use Quest are never pulled into it.

**Does life design cost anything?** Quest does not lock life design behind a plan: the questions, the grouped quest list and moving quests work on every plan, and Quest is free forever. For plan limits on other AI features, see [Plans and pricing](/reference/plans).

esoi_brief.title: Quest and ESOI: in plain words
esoi_brief.text:
Quest is designed with a framework called **Evolvable Structure that Optimizes Intent** (ESOI). This section describes the Quest product in ESOI's terms: what Quest is for, what it is defined to do, and where each part of a quest fits. It describes the product as people use it, not how it is built.

## ESOI in plain words

You do not need these terms to use Quest, but they explain why creating a quest asks what it does.

ESOI is a way of writing a goal down so that it can be planned, tested and improved. For any intention, it asks five things:

| Plain question | ESOI record | Where you meet it in Quest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is in the way? | **Problem** | Current state, and the problems Quest lists in Grounded Strategies |
| What do I want, and why does it matter? | **Ideal** | Your vision and purpose; your preferences become the principles every strategy must honor |
| What are the ways I could handle it? | **Solution** | Grounded Strategies |
| How will I carry a strategy out? | **Implementation** | Your habits and goals, and the experiments that test them |
| How will I know it is working? | **Metric** | Measurable outcomes, and what an experiment records |

"Evolvable" means the written structure is not fixed. As your results come in, the strategies, the plan and even the intention can change.

A **quest** is one instance of this for one intention of yours. That is why it is never a to-do list: a to-do list holds tasks, and a quest holds the reasons, the obstacles, the strategies and the measures behind them. An **experiment** is a small intention inside your quest, a test of which way of carrying out a strategy works for you. The five-step creation flow collects these parts one at a time: see [Why creating a quest is so detailed](/getting-started/your-first-quest#why-creating-a-quest-is-so-detailed) and [Experiments](/guide/experiments#experiments-in-plain-words).

experiments_intro.title: Experiments
experiments_intro.text:
# Experiments

Quest stands for **Qualitative Understanding Enables Self-Transformation**. The Experiments section on a quest's dashboard is where that becomes literal. You ask a research question about your quest, see what existing evidence says about it, then test the answer in your own life and let the AI read what your data shows.

## Experiments in plain words

### What an experiment is

An experiment is a small test, run in your own life, of one way of reaching your goal. You pick a question ("Which breakfast supports my long runs?"), do something for a while, record what happens, and Quest shows what your own record says. In [ESOI](/esoi/), the framework Quest is built on (Evolvable Structure that Optimizes Intent, which writes a goal down as an intention you can test and improve), an experiment is a small intention inside your quest: it compares ways of carrying out a strategy and keeps the one your data supports.

### How to run one

1. **While creating a quest:** in step 4, **Experiments**, Quest proposes experiments for the strategies you kept. Tick **Run this experiment** on the ones you want and continue, or choose **Skip experiments**.
2. **Any time later:** open your quest, go to its **Experiments** section, and choose **Suggest an experiment with AI**, or **Add research question** to write your own.
3. **Live it:** do the linked habits and goals, and log each entry with the fields the experiment asks for (and a line on how it felt).
4. **Read the result:** tap **Analyze my data**. When you are convinced, write your conclusion (**Write conclusion**).

The worked example below follows one experiment from start to finish.

### What it does for your progress

A plan tells you what to do. An experiment tells you whether it is working for you. Instead of guessing which strategy fits, you test it and decide from your own record. When an experiment was drafted for a strategy, its results move that strategy's confidence on the strategy card, and Quest can suggest changes to your plan that your data points to. You accept or dismiss each one, and nothing changes until you do. A conclusion goes back into your plan and your weekly reflection, so the quest improves as evidence arrives instead of staying a fixed list.

### Who it suits

- People who have more than one plausible way to reach a goal and want to know which works for them.
- People who are willing to log a little data each time they do the thing (a number, a rating, a sentence).
- Anyone whose goal shows up in something they can record. A goal you cannot observe in any way is harder to test.

If you would rather not log anything, you do not need experiments: you can skip them when you create a quest and still have the full plan.

### Common questions

**What is an experiment?** One question about your own life, tested by doing something and recording the result. See above.

**Do I need to run experiments to have a quest?** No. **Skip experiments** moves on with none, and you can add one later.

**Do I need research or statistics skills?** No. Quest computes the numbers from your entries and the AI explains them in words, with a confidence level and its limits.

**How much data is enough?** Several entries on each side of the comparison. Two runs each is a start, not an answer, and the confidence level says so.

**Does the AI decide for me?** No. Analysis text is marked as written by the AI, and changes to your plan wait for your yes.

**Can Quest help me design one?** Yes. Tap **Discuss with AI** on a question, or ask Quest AI in a chat on the quest.

There are two ways to answer a question, and the best experiments use both:

- **Existing evidence.** Tap **Run deep inquiry** to research the question across research papers and real lived experiences, the same way quest creation does.
- **Your own life.** Link the habits, collections and goals that gather data for the question, then tap **Analyze my data**.

mentee_find.title: Mentors: what a mentor is and finding one
mentee_find.text:
# Mentors

A mentor is a real person who guides you through your quest with check-ins and a private chat. Quest connects people who want guidance with people who offer it, and handles the scheduling and the payment around it.

Mentorship has two sides, and one account can be on both. This page has a section for each:

- [Mentors for mentees](#mentors-for-mentees): finding a mentor, requesting one, paying, check-ins, and what a mentor can see.
- [Mentors for people who mentor](#mentors-for-people-who-mentor): applying, getting listed, setting prices, inviting your own clients, check-ins and earnings.

Mentors are optional. Many people run quests with only the AI and the community. A mentor adds human accountability and judgment when you want it. Everything starts on the **Mentorship** page: open **Mentorship** in the navigation menu (under Explore), or the **Mentors** chip in the Community tab. It lists your conversations in four sections (**All**, **Mentors** for the people mentoring you, **Mentees** for the people you mentor, and **Requests** for people asking you to mentor them), with **Find a mentor** and **Become a mentor** at the top.

## Mentors for mentees

### Mentee: what it is

A mentor is someone who has done what you are working toward and works with you on your quest. Quest's own words for it: "Learn from someone who has already done what you are working toward." You get regular check-ins on a rhythm you and the mentor agree, and a private chat between them. If you choose, the mentor can open the quests you share and see your real plan and progress, so the conversation does not start from zero each time.

You decide what a mentor sees. Nothing is shared until you choose it, and you can stop at any time.

### Finding a mentor

Open **Mentorship** and tap **Find a mentor**. A guided search opens. If you want to know how it works first, tap **How being a mentee works**.

1. **Describe what you want help with.** The box asks "What do you want help with?" Write a sentence in your own words (for example, switching careers into design) or start from a topic: Career, Meditation and mindfulness, Health and fitness, Relationships, Creativity, Spiritual growth, Money and business, or Learning a skill. Type at least three characters, then tap **Search**. Search reads the meaning of what you write, so a sentence about your goal works as well as a keyword.
2. **Look at the mentors.** Each result shows the mentor's background, focus areas, a verification badge (see below) and a line such as "From $40 per check-in". Tap a mentor to open their **Mentor Profile**, with their About, Expertise and Check-ins.
3. **Request the mentor.** Tap **Request this mentor**. Choose a check-in tier, choose how often to check in (**Weekly**, **Every two weeks** or **Monthly**), and add an optional note about what you want help with. Tap **Request this mentor** again to send it.
4. **Start.** Mentors who accept everyone start at once ("You are now working with ..."). If a mentor answers each request, you see "Request sent" and are notified when it is accepted. Until then you can withdraw the request with **Withdraw request**, and nothing has been charged.

Requesting a mentor does not charge you. You are charged only when a check-in takes place.

**The verification badge.** Every listed mentor has a score from 0 to 100 from an AI read of their application. You see the overall percentage and a plain label: **Strong** (75 to 100), **Pass** (50 to 74), or **Not yet verified** (below 50). A mentor whose score is still being worked out shows "Verification in progress". The score describes how well a mentor's stated experience is backed up. It is information to help you choose, not a guarantee, so read the profile too.

mentee_pay.title: Mentors: paying a mentor
mentee_pay.text:
### Paying a mentor

There is no subscription to a mentor and you never type in an amount. You add dollar credit to your own balance by card, and credit is spent on a mentor only when a check-in takes place.

- **Add credit.** In **Settings**, open **Billing & Subscription**, find the **Mentorship** card and tap **Add credits**. Choose $20, $50 or $100, or enter another amount (at least $5, at most $10,000), then **Continue to payment**. When you request a mentor and your balance is short, the app also offers **Add credits** right there. This is a one-time payment, not a recurring charge. Money you added by card is used first, then any credit you have earned. Card money cannot be withdrawn as cash. Unused credit stays in your balance. On a phone, the card page opens inside the app and closes by itself when you finish or cancel; Quest then waits for your payment to arrive and tells you when the credit has been added, which can take a few seconds. If you close the page yourself, nothing is wrong: if you did pay, the credit appears shortly.
- **Choose a tier.** A mentor offers one or more check-in tiers. A tier is a named package with one fixed price per check-in, and you pick the one you want when you request the mentor. You need at least that tier's total in your balance to request the mentor. If you do not have enough, the app asks you to add credit. Requesting a mentor does not charge you.
- **A mentor's own price for you.** A mentor can set a price for you personally, including Free. When they have, you do not pick a tier: **Your price with** the mentor is shown on the request and under your mentors. Free means nothing is charged and you need no credit.
- **Service fee.** On the Free and Quest AI plans, each check-in carries a 5% service fee on top of the mentor's price, so your mentor always receives their full price. On Quest Guided there is no fee. When you request a mentor, schedule a check-in or look at your check-ins, the app shows you the total, with the fee on its own line.
- **Credit is spent at the check-in.** When your mentor submits a check-in, or you confirm one that took place outside the app, that tier's price plus any service fee is taken from your balance. If your credit does not cover it, the check-in still counts, the payment is held, and adding credit releases it.
- **Say thank you.** You can also send your mentor a one-off payment with a short note, for example to thank them for an extra session (**Send a thank-you payment**, from $1, note required). It is separate from the tiers, comes out of your balance the same way, and needs enough credit when you send it.

How often you meet is agreed with the mentor.

mentee_working.title: Mentors: working with a mentor
mentee_working.text:
### Working with a mentor

Once connected, you have a direct chat with your mentor for the back and forth between check-ins. Use the dropdown above the message box to tag a message with one of your quests. Only the two of you can read the chat.

**Check-ins.** Open **Check-ins** from the chat header. Tap the plus button, **Schedule a check-in**, to pick a date and time with your mentor (either of you can schedule one). The tabs are **Upcoming**, **Completed** and **All**. Check-ins are scheduled in Quest and your mentor marks each one **Complete**. If a check-in happened outside the app, tap **Confirm it happened** and the same payment is made. To cancel a check-in, tap **Cancel**: nothing is charged.

You choose which of your quests your mentor can open, one quest at a time, under My mentors (open it from **Settings**, under Privacy, with **Manage mentor sharing**, or tap **Choose quests to share** on a mentor in the Mentors section). Each quest is Not shared, View (your mentor sees the whole quest dashboard but cannot change it) or Edit (your mentor can also edit it). Your mentor sees only the quests you share, and you can change or stop sharing at any time. With a quest shared, the conversation stays grounded in your actual plan and progress.

A mentor supports and advises you. You still own your quest and your decisions. A mentor can propose changes to a quest you share (a **Mentor Suggestion**, with the reason and the current and suggested text side by side). You **Accept** or **Decline** it, and a decline needs a short reason.

If you choose it for a metric (How this is recorded, My mentor drafts or Either), a mentor of a quest you shared can propose a value for it. Their proposal appears on that metric for you to confirm or correct, and nothing is written into your collections until you do. Mentors see these requests on their dashboard.

**Ending a mentorship.** Open the mentor's profile and tap **Cancel mentorship**. Access to your quests ends at once, scheduled check-ins are cancelled with no charge, and check-ins already completed stay paid (nothing is refunded).

mentor_become.title: Mentors: becoming a mentor
mentor_become.text:
### Mentor: what it is

Becoming a mentor lets you guide people on Quest for pay. You set your own check-in tiers and prices, bring clients you already work with through your own invite link, and are found by mentees who describe what they need. Quest handles scheduling, the credit your clients pay with, and payouts.

### Becoming a mentor

Open **Mentorship** and tap **Become a mentor** (the button then reads **Start your application**, or **Continue your application** if you began one). The mentor page that explains how it works has an **Apply to mentor** button too. Your answers save as you go, so you can stop and come back. The application has four steps:

1. **Context ("Share what you have").** Everything here is optional. Add a resume, certificates, links to your profiles (LinkedIn, your website) or a few lines about yourself, and Quest reads them to fill in the next steps for you. Some sites, LinkedIn most often, cannot be read without signing in; Quest tells you when that happens and you can paste the text instead. Anything Quest fills in is marked "Filled from your documents, please check", and you check and edit everything before anything is sent.
2. **Account ("Your account details").** Your name, email, phone, country, city, current occupation, years of experience and primary area of expertise. You also agree to the Mentor Guidelines and Terms of Service.
3. **Profile ("Set up your mentor profile").** Your profile photo (PNG or JPEG, at least 400x400 px), professional headline, About you, Mentor bio, categories, languages, time zone, available days and hours, and preferred mentoring formats (One-on-One, Chat, Video calls, Group sessions, Audio calls). This is what mentees see when choosing a mentor.
4. **Credentials ("Verify your expertise").** Certifications, professional licences, a portfolio or website, your LinkedIn profile, years of professional experience, client testimonials (client name, occupation, relationship and their words), and any supporting documents such as award letters or press mentions. You need at least one thing that can be checked: a certification, a licence, a testimonial, or a link to your portfolio or LinkedIn. Then tap **Submit Application**.

**You are listed as soon as you submit.** No person has to approve you first. An AI then reads your application and scores it from 0 to 100, usually within a minute or two, and writes a reason for each score. Quest's own wording: "Scored by AI, usually within a minute or two. Listed straight away. No approval wait."

The score has five checks: **Profile verified**, **Identity checked** (this is about consistency across your application, not an identity document), **Certifications reviewed**, **Experience evaluated** and **Testimonials processed**. Each check passes at 50 or above. A check you had nothing to submit for, such as certifications or testimonials, shows **Not provided** and is left out of the total. The AI also places you at a level that reflects your experience, shown on your dashboard as your current level.

- **What mentees see.** Your overall percentage and a plain label (**Strong** 75 to 100, **Pass** 50 to 74, **Not yet verified** below 50). They do not see the documents you uploaded or the written reasons.
- **What you see.** Open **See your verification** (or the **Your verification** card on your dashboard) to read each check with its reason.
- **A low score does not remove you.** A score below 50 does not unlist you on its own. Your badge reads Not yet verified, and the Quest team may take a look. The team can also hide a profile after a review, and it writes the reason for you. While a profile is hidden, your invite link stops working, you cannot complete check-ins and you cannot see your payouts. You can ask for a review by writing to the support address shown on your status screen.
- **If scoring is unavailable.** If Quest cannot score your application, you stay listed and the badge reads Verification unavailable.
- **Who reads your application.** The AI scorer reads it, and the Quest team can look at it when a score needs a second look. Your name, email, country, city and photo are not sent to the scorer.

account_profile.title: Account settings: profile, appearance and time
account_profile.text:
Manage your profile, privacy, notifications, and data from **Settings** in the app. Open it from the **Profile** tab: choose **Settings**. This page is an overview of what is there. The screen's sections include **Account**, **Timezone**, **Language**, **Notifications**, **Calendar & Scheduling**, **Weekly Reflections**, **Privacy**, **AI Tasks**, **Appearance**, a second **Account** section with **Logout** and **Delete Account**, and **Help & Support**.

## Profile

In **Settings > Account**, **Profile & Identity** ("Manage your name, photo, and bio") opens your account screen. There you can:

- Tap your picture (it has a small camera on it) to upload a profile photo, and tap **Remove Photo** to take it off.
- Set your **Display Name**. It is the name shown in chats (Galaxy, Planet, Town, and Mentor or Mentee). If you leave it blank, your character name is used, and if you have neither, your first name.
- Edit your **Bio**.
- Change your **Real Name** (under **Account Name**), which is stored securely with your account.
- See your **Email**, which cannot be changed because it identifies your account.

This is separate from your community [character](/guide/communities#your-character), which is the identity (name, bio, and 3D avatar) you use in towns and planets.

**Billing & Subscription** in the same section manages your plan and payments (see [Plans and pricing](/reference/plans)). **Life Design** appears there too once it is available (see [Life design](/guide/life-design)).

## Appearance and time

- **Appearance:** choose **Light** or **Dark**. Your choice is saved and synced across devices.
- **Timezone:** set your time zone, or leave it on **Auto-detect**, which shows your current one. Your Today, Schedule, and period reviews use it to decide what counts as today, this week, and so on.

account_language.title: Account settings: language
account_language.text:
## Language

Quest's interface is available in two languages: **English** and **Español**. No other language ships today.

**Where to choose it.** In **Settings**, tap the **Language** row (it shows your current language). A **Select Language** list opens: tap the language you want, and the app switches right away, no restart needed. Before you sign in, the public pages (welcome, sign in, sign up and the marketing pages) have a language dropdown too; whatever you pick there is saved to your account when you sign up or sign in. Your choice is saved with your account, so it carries over to every device you sign into.

**What changes.**

- The interface: navigation, buttons, labels, error messages, onboarding, and settings.
- Quest's world content: planet, town, and category names and descriptions, and the built-in character species. New ones created later are translated automatically too.
- What Quest AI writes for you. Every piece of text Quest's AI authors (chat replies, plans, suggestions, intents) follows the language set in **Settings > Language**. It does this even when your notes or quests are in another language, and it keeps the names and titles you wrote exactly as written.

**What does not change.** What you have written: your quest titles, notes, and descriptions always display in the language you wrote them in.

**Brand names.** "Quest", "Quest AI" and "Spiritual Data" stay in English in every language.

If a translation is not ready yet for a piece of text, Quest shows it in English rather than leaving a blank.

**Common questions**

*I write to Quest AI in Español but my language is set to English. Which does it use?* The setting. Quest AI replies in the language chosen in **Settings > Language**. Set it to Español to get replies in Español, or ask it explicitly for another language in your message.

*Will my existing quests be translated?* No. They stay in the language you wrote them.

account_notifications.title: Account settings: notifications
account_notifications.text:
## Notifications

The bell in the header opens your **Notifications** page: everything Quest has told you, in one list.

- **Filter at the top:** All, Quests (asks, AI task results, goal and habit reminders, quest invitations), Social (mentor messages, chat replies and mentions, community activity) and System (account, bookings, data). Each filter shows how many unread items it holds.
- **Each row says what a tap does**, for example "Open ask", "Open AI task", "Open habit" or "Open team chat". A notification with nowhere to go says "Tap to mark read" instead.
- **Remove a notification** with the X on its row. You get five seconds to Undo before it is gone for good. **Clear** removes read notifications, or all of them, after you confirm. Unread chats are not stored notifications, so they stay in the list until you open the chat.
- **Mark all read** clears every unread badge at once. Older notifications load with **Show older notifications**.
- The gear in the page header opens the notification settings below.

### Notification settings

Open them with the gear on the Notifications page, or from **Settings > Notifications > Notification Preferences** ("Email, push, sound, and category settings"). Everything below starts on, except where noted. The screen has these parts, top to bottom:

- **Enable Notifications:** the master switch. Turning it off silences everything at once.
- **Notification Channels:** how Quest reaches you. **Email Notifications** sends Quest updates by email. **Push Notifications** sends alerts to your device, and covers the habit and goal reminders Quest schedules for your set times, so turning it off silences those as well. With push off, notifications still appear in your Notifications list.
- **Scheduled Reminders:** **Habit & Goal Reminders** (reminders at the scheduled times for habits and goals) and **Alarm-Style Reminders** (let habits with alarms ring as full alarms; turn it off to get regular reminders instead, and each habit's own alarm setting is kept).
- **When I review asks:** off until you turn it on. Pick the days, time and length of your regular look at your [asks](/guide/teams), and Quest emails you one digest of open asks before it (you choose how far ahead: 1, 2 or 4 hours). Teammates' notice asks then default their deadline to the end of your next review time.
- **Next actions email:** off until you turn it on. Quest AI writes one short email on the days you pick: what is overdue or due soon, the asks waiting on you, and the outcomes that are behind. It sends nothing on a day when there is nothing to report, and at most one email a day. **Preview my digest** shows what it would say right now without sending anything. The days and time start as weekdays at 9:00; set your timezone in the same card.
- **Notification Categories:** choose which types you want: **Habits**, **Quests**, **Mentors**, **Community**, **Town Chat**, **Planet Chat**, **Galaxy Chat** (replies and @mentions), **Data**, and **System** (account, billing, and security).
- **Notification Behavior:** **Sound** and **Vibration** switches, and a row that opens your browser or device notification permissions.
- **Notification Devices:** see every phone and browser registered to your account, pick which one is primary (only the primary device receives notifications, to avoid duplicates), register the device you are on with **Register This Device**, and remove any you no longer use.

If notifications do not arrive on a phone, check that Quest is allowed to send notifications in your device's own settings, and that Do Not Disturb or Focus is not silencing it.

Quest has no scheduled quiet hours setting. To silence notifications for a while, turn off **Enable Notifications** or the channel you do not want.

calendar_google.title: Calendar Sync: connect Google Calendar
calendar_google.text:
Under **Add an account**, tap **Connect Google** (its accessibility name is Connect Google Calendar) and sign in with your Google account in the browser. This is a direct connection between Quest's servers and Google, so once it is set up it keeps syncing on its own even when the app is closed. If the connection is not set up on the server you use, the row says "Google Calendar connection is not configured yet." and the button is not offered.

After connecting, the account's card lists your Google calendars under **Your Google calendars** ("Turn on a calendar to sync it with Quest"). Turn on the ones you want; each becomes its own connection with its own settings, and a calendar marked **Primary** or **Read-only** says so. A calendar that is read-only in your Google account (for example, one someone shared with you) can still bring its events into Quest, but Quest cannot write your schedule to it. A fresh Google connection starts exactly like a fresh device one: nothing syncs until you turn a direction on (see "What a fresh connection does" above).

Google calendars stay in step on their own, in both directions. Changes you make in Quest (a goal or habit created, moved, retitled, abandoned or deleted, including when its quest is deleted) reach Google within a few seconds, and so does changing a calendar's settings, such as turning on Sync goals. Completing a goal does not change its Google event, which stays as it was. Changes you make in Google appear in Quest within about a minute while you have **Schedule** open, with nothing to tap or reload, and about every 15 minutes the rest of the time, even with the app closed. Each connected Google account card has one **Sync now** button that runs a full sync of its active calendars immediately and tells you what it found. It is the quickest way to check that a calendar you just connected, or just reconnected, is really working. If Google cannot be reached, the calendar says so on its own row and tries again by itself; Sync now says the same instead of reporting that everything is up to date.

calendar_where.title: Calendar Sync: where your events show up
calendar_where.text:
## Where your events show up

Events from every calendar with "Show events on Quest and use for AI scheduling" on appear on **Today** and on **Schedule**, in their real time slots, next to your goals and habits. If a calendar you turned on shows nothing, that setting is where to look first.

They look different on purpose. A calendar event is drawn as a muted, outlined block with a small calendar icon and the word Calendar, so you can tell at a glance what Quest is asking of you and what the rest of your life is asking of you. Events that last all day, like a birthday or a day off, sit in a compact strip across the top of the day instead of taking up the whole timeline. An event you marked Free rather than Busy is drawn lighter still: it is there, but it is not claiming the time.

**Calendar events are not editable in Quest.** Tap one and you get its title, its time, which calendar it came from, and a note saying you change it where you made it (plus a line saying so when the event is marked Free). There are no actions on it at all: you cannot drag it to a new time, check it off, or delete it here, because it does not belong to Quest. Change it in the calendar you made it in and Quest picks the change up on the next sync. If you want to work with it in Quest, turn on **Create goals from calendar events** for that calendar and it becomes a goal or a habit you own.

account_delete.title: Delete your account
account_delete.text:
**This action cannot be undone.** Once deleted, your data cannot be recovered.

**Want a copy first?** Export your Data Collections before you delete: each collection exports to CSV, JSON, TXT, or PDF (see [Your data and the API](/reference/developers#exporting)).

**Have a paid plan?** Cancel it first. If you subscribed through the Apple App Store or Google Play, see [Premium Subscriptions](#premium-subscriptions) below. If you subscribed on the web, open **Settings > Billing & Subscription** and choose **Manage subscription**.

### Step 1: Open Settings

1. Open the Quest app (or the web app) and go to the **Profile** tab.
2. Choose **Settings**.

### Step 2: Find Delete Account

1. Scroll down to the **Account** section near the bottom (it holds **Logout** and **Delete Account**).
2. Tap **Delete Account**, shown in red with the line "Permanently delete your account and all data".

### Step 3: Review What Will Be Deleted

A box titled **Delete Your Account?** opens. It shows:
- A warning that the action is "permanent and cannot be undone", and the list of what you will lose.
- A note that your data will be permanently removed from our servers within 30 days (except for anonymized analytics required by law).
- **Your data summary**: how many quests, collections, entries, deep inquiries and town memberships will be deleted, and a total.
- An optional **Why are you leaving?** question. You can pick one reason: No longer using the app, Found a better alternative, Privacy concerns, Too many notifications, Not achieving my goals, Taking a break from goal tracking, or Other.

Tap **Continue** to go on, or **Cancel** to stop.

### Step 4: Confirm Deletion

1. In the **Final Confirmation** box, type `DELETE MY ACCOUNT` exactly as shown, in capitals.
2. The **Delete My Account** button turns on only when the words match. Tap it.
3. Wait while Quest shows "Deleting your account..." and do not close the app. It can take a moment.

## Data Retention Policy

- Your data is permanently removed from our servers within 30 days of account deletion.
- Some anonymized analytics data may be retained for service improvement and where the law requires it.
- An anonymized audit record of the deletion (not tied to you) is kept for compliance purposes.

## Premium Subscriptions

If you have an active premium subscription:
- **Apple App Store**: Your subscription will continue until you cancel it through your Apple ID settings. Go to Settings > [Your Name] > Subscriptions on your iPhone to cancel.
- **Google Play**: Your subscription will continue until you cancel it through Google Play. Go to Google Play Store > Menu > Subscriptions to cancel.

Deleting your Quest account does not automatically cancel your subscription with Apple or Google. Please cancel your subscription separately to avoid future charges. See [Plans and pricing](/reference/plans#billing-notes).

exporting.title: Your data and the API: exporting
exporting.text:
## Exporting

You do not need the API to get your data out. Any [Data Collection](/data-collections/#exporting-your-data) exports to **CSV, JSON, TXT, or PDF** from the app: from a collection's export button, or several at once from the collections list. A quest can also be exported as a PDF (see [Spec library](/guide/spec-library)). The app has no single button that exports your whole account. For programmatic access to the rest, including all your collections at once, use the API below.

quest_ai_intro.title: Quest AI: what it is and which kind of AI task for what
quest_ai_intro.text:
# Quest AI

Quest AI is the assistant built into the app. It is a single chat that knows your quests, your plans, and your progress, so you can ask for help in plain language instead of clicking through screens.

You reach it from **Quest AI** in the navigation. It opens as a general chat by default, and you can point it at a specific quest when you want it focused there.

## Why a chat that knows your quests

A chat window is where you talk. Quest is the structure and data underneath: plans, habits and collections you can edit directly. Quest AI sits on top of that structure, so it works from your actual goals instead of a blank page, and it can make the changes for you. You spend less time updating Quest and more time doing the work in it. When a job is too big or too slow for a conversation, you hand it to your AI as a task, follow its progress, and it asks you in one place when it needs your decision.

**Who it suits.** Anyone who would rather say "add a habit to meditate every weekday morning" than open four screens. People who think out loud (use [Voice Mode](/guide/voice-mode)). People with more to do than hands to do it, who want research, drafting or a recurring pass over a quest done in the background. People new to Quest who want to ask how a feature works.

## Which kind of AI task for what

Pick by what you are asking for. You never choose a type by name: you say what you want, and Quest AI picks the route. The type shows on the work afterwards (see [Types of AI task](/guide/ai-tasks#types-of-ai-task)).

| You want | Say something like | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A change to your Quest data now | "Add a goal to call the dentist this week" | Runs in the chat after you approve it (or at once with **Auto-run** on). Recorded as a **Quest operation** task. |
| Today's facts from the web | "What is the current price of ..." | Quest AI searches while you wait ("Searching the web...") and cites its sources. No task is created. |
| Web research that takes time, or should wait | "Overnight, research three standing desks under $400 and report back" | Becomes an AI task of type **Web search**. |
| Work over your own documents, no internet needed | "Tomorrow, go through my context documents and draft the summary" | Becomes an AI task of type **Docs lookup**. |
| Work on your team's server or connected computer | "Check the server logs for errors" | When your team has a runner connected, becomes an AI task of type **External environment**, sent to that runner. |
| How Quest works | "How do I connect Google Calendar?" | Answered in the chat from Quest's own documentation. This is the one thing the Free plan chat does. |
| What the research says | Open **Science**, or ask for a Deep Inquiry on a quest | See [Science](/guide/science) and [Deep Inquiries](/guide/deep-inquiries). |
| The same pass again and again | "Every Monday, summarize my week" | A task with a repeat schedule, or **Autopilot** on the quest. See [AI Tasks](/guide/ai-tasks#autopilot). |
| Steps in a fixed order, with owners and times | "Create a workflow for this quest" | A [Workflow](/guide/workflows): steps joined by arrows, each starting after the one before. |

To force the route, say so: "make a task for it", "hand this to my AI" or "use a deep run" always creates a task, whatever the work is about. Without such a cue, anything Quest AI can answer or do right now it does right now, and only work you defer ("tomorrow", "overnight", "in the background", "every Monday") or that needs the live web becomes a task.

## The Free plan and paid plans

- **Free.** Quest AI chat and [Voice Mode](/guide/voice-mode) answer questions about how Quest works, from Quest's documentation. The chat shows "You're on the free plan, so Quest AI can only answer from product documentation." It does not read or change your quests, search the web, read attachments, hand off AI tasks, or help with general questions, writing, research or coaching. When you ask for one of those it says what Quest AI would do for it and shows a **Subscribe** button. Free chat also has a small daily allowance; at the limit the chat says "You've reached today's chat limit."
- **31 day trial, Quest AI and Quest Guided.** Everything on this page: chat that reads and changes your quests, web search, attachments, AI tasks and voice. Chat has a generous daily allowance on these plans meant as a safeguard, not a limit for normal use.
- **Try it once, free.** For each paid AI feature you have never used, Quest invites you to subscribe and shows **Try it once, free**: one sitting of about 30 minutes that runs the feature for real. See [Plans and pricing](/reference/plans).

## What you can ask

Quest AI answers questions and takes actions on your quests. For example:

- "Explain what this strategy is based on."
- "Add a habit to meditate 10 minutes every weekday morning."
- "My schedule changed. Rework this plan around weekends only."
- "Summarize where I am on my fitness quest."
- "Suggest a goal for next week based on how this week went."

Replies are formatted for easy reading, and you will see a working indicator while it thinks. Requests that change a quest, like adding a goal, happen right there in the chat.

quest_ai_web.title: Quest AI: current information from the web
quest_ai_web.text:
## Current information from the web

When a question depends on something that changes in the world, like a release date, a price, a race schedule, or the latest version of a tool, Quest AI looks it up on the web before answering. You will see "Searching the web…" while it does, and "Reading a web page…" when it needs the full text of one page. You can also paste a link to a public page and ask about it.

Answers that use the web cite their sources as links right in the reply, so you can open the page and check it yourself. In [Voice Mode](/guide/voice-mode), the links stay in the transcript and only the words are spoken.

Quest AI does not search the web for your own quests, goals, or notes, or for small talk. Those answers come from your Quest data. If web search is unavailable, Quest AI answers from what it already knows and tells you the information may be out of date.

quest_ai_now_later.title: Quest AI: doing work now, or later
quest_ai_now_later.text:
## Doing work now, or later

Some requests are quick and run in the moment. Others are open-ended and take time. Quest AI can handle both.

- **In the moment:** "add a goal to this quest" runs inline and you see the result immediately.
- **Handed off:** when you ask for something to be done later, overnight, or on a schedule ("research three standing desks under $400 and report back", "draft my weekly update tomorrow morning"), Quest AI recognizes the hand-off and turns it into a task for your assistant. You can watch its progress and read the result when it is done.

Handing work off is part of the [Productivity workflow](/guide/productivity), which also covers the **Tasks for your AI** switch (Settings, AI Tasks; on unless you turned it off), scheduling tasks, and reviewing what your assistant did.

### When the work is not finished

A handed-off task checks its own result against what you asked. If the first try falls short, it retries within the same task, with feedback on what was missing and a stronger model, until the check passes or its attempt and cost limits run out. If a person is needed it stops and asks you instead of guessing. A task that ran but never reached its goal ends as **Not fully done**, not Done, with what is missing written at the end of its result. To carry on, send a message in the task's message box, which continues the work with its full context. There is no setting that starts another task automatically when a goal is not met: you decide the next step. See [Follow-up and ordered work](/guide/ai-tasks#follow-up-and-ordered-work).

ai_tasks_intro.title: AI Tasks: what they are
ai_tasks_intro.text:
# AI Tasks

AI Tasks are pieces of work you hand to your AI to do in the background. You delegate a task, the AI works on it, and it reports back when it is done. You do not have to wait around. You can keep using Quest while it works, and check on the result later.

**Why it exists.** A chat answers while you wait. A task is for the work that should not make you wait: research, drafting, a recurring pass over a quest. You hand your AI a job, follow its progress, and it asks you in one place when it needs your decision. The point is to carry part of the load, so your attention stays on what matters. AI Tasks are part of the 31 day trial, Quest AI and Quest Guided. On the Free plan you can try them once.

**Who it suits.** People with more to do than time, who can describe a job in a sentence. Someone who wants three standing desks compared by morning, a weekly summary of a quest, or a draft to react to rather than a blank page. Teams, where each person's AI works their own lane. It suits least the work only you can do (a conversation, a decision about taste): for that, ask for a draft or an ask for yourself.

There are four ways a task gets created:

- **From your daily reflection.** The "Tasks for your AI" field turns each line you write into a queued task.
- **From the + button.** On the AI Tasks page, tap the **+** button (tooltip: Delegate a task) and write what you want done. The AI Tasks row in the menu also carries a **+** and a microphone: the microphone opens **Voice AI task**, where you speak what you want and tap **Continue to AI task** to reach the same form with your words filled in.
- **From Quest AI chat.** When you ask for something open-ended or scheduled, like "research three standing desks under $400 and report back tomorrow", Quest AI turns it into a task instead of answering inline. The task gets its title, quest, team and environment filled in the same way the **Delegate to AI** form fills them, so it lands on the right quest even when you asked from a general chat.

When a chat request needs your team's server or runner environment (checking server logs, running something on that machine, work only that environment can do), Quest AI routes the task to that environment automatically, even from a general chat with no quest selected. And when one message bundles clearly separate pieces of work (say, a server check and some web research), Quest AI splits it into one task per piece, each with its own live card in the chat, so you can follow, open, or cancel each part on its own.

When several of your quests are in the chat and Quest AI cannot tell which one a task belongs to, it asks once, listing up to three of them and offering "no quest". Answer with the quest's name or number, or say "no quest" (or ask for an independent or standalone task up front) and the task is created without one. You can also name any quest of your own, even one that is not part of this chat. Quest AI never asks the same question twice in a row: if your answer still does not match a quest, it creates the task without a quest, says which name it could not find, and you can attach it later by giving the exact quest name.
- **From team chat.** Tap **Make this a task** on any AI team member's message to queue that message as a real task. A confirmation reads "Queued as an AI task." A "View task" link appears once it is queued.

For how delegation fits the wider rhythm of planning and reviewing, see the [Productivity workflow](/guide/productivity).

ai_tasks_types.title: AI Tasks: types of AI task
ai_tasks_types.text:
## Types of AI task

Every task has a type, shown on its row, in its header and as a chip in chat, and you can filter the list by it. You do not pick the type. Quest AI reads your request, decides what the work needs, and routes it.

- **Quest operation.** A change to your Quest data made from chat: adding a goal, logging a habit, saving a note, reworking a plan. It runs in the chat behind an approve or undo card and is recorded here so you can find it. It also covers general deep work that needs no web, documents or computer, such as drafting or planning. How to ask: say it in chat ("add a goal to ...").
- **Web search.** Work that needs the live internet: research, comparing options, finding people or prices. It runs in the background and reports back. How to ask: "Overnight, research the best standing desks under $400 and draft me a comparison." For a quick fact you need now, Quest AI searches the web inside the reply instead and creates no task.
- **Docs lookup.** Work over your own context documents and knowledge, with no internet. How to ask: name your documents ("go through my notes on the grant and list the open questions"). This is different from asking how Quest works: that is answered in chat from Quest's own documentation and creates no task.
- **External environment.** A deep run on one of your team's connected runners, for work only that machine can do: server logs, files on it, running something there. It needs a team with a runner set up. How to ask: "check the server logs for errors" in a chat for that team, or pin the task to an environment in the form.
- **Other.** Older tasks recorded before types existed, shown on the task itself as **Background task**.

**Science and research questions.** Papers and first-hand experiences are in [Science](/guide/science), not in a task. In chat, a research question that needs fresh sources becomes a Web search, and evidence for one of your quests is a [Deep Inquiry](/guide/deep-inquiries). See [How-to: research and evidence](/how-to/research-and-evidence).

**Standing work.** Run the same pass again and again with a repeat schedule on the task, or with [Autopilot](#autopilot) on a quest.

ai_tasks_followup.title: AI Tasks: follow-up and ordered work
ai_tasks_followup.text:
## Follow-up and ordered work

**Several tasks in a row.** Tasks do not wait on each other. There is no setting that says "run B when A is done". Three ways to get an order:

1. **One task, steps in order.** Write the steps in the order you want inside one request. One task is one piece of work with one result.
2. **A checklist in chat.** Ask Quest AI for a checklist and tap the boxes in the order you want. Each tap starts its own task (see [Tap a checklist item to start it](/guide/quest-ai#tap-a-checklist-item-to-start-it)). Quest does not hold a later item back for an earlier one.
3. **A Workflow.** For steps with owners, times and a real order, build a [Workflow](/guide/workflows): steps joined by arrows, where a step can be set to start once the step before it is done. A step given to an AI representative hands its instructions to your AI as a task at its time. Workflows are part of the paid plans.

When one message bundles clearly separate pieces of work, Quest AI makes one task per piece (up to three). Those run side by side, not in sequence.

**When a goal is not met.** Before a task reports, its result is checked against what you asked.

- If the result falls short, the AI tries again inside the same task, told what was missing, on a stronger model if needed. It stops when the check passes, when its attempt and cost limits are reached, when two attempts end the same way with nothing new done, when a tool it needs keeps failing, or when only a person can close the gap.
- A task that ran but did not reach its goal ends as **Not fully done**. The end of its result says what was not verified and what to do next. If a person is needed it ends as **Needs your input** with an ask.
- To carry on, open the task and send a message in its box. That starts a follow-up on the same thread, with full context. Or tap the **+** in the task header to start a fresh task prefilled with the same quest and team. Answering an ask resumes the work automatically as a follow-up.
- An Autopilot pass reads the last run on its quest and treats a Not fully done run as an attempt, not a settled answer, so the next pass can finish it. See [Each pass picks up where the last one left off](#autopilot).

Quest does not start a new task on its own when a goal is not met, and there is no way to say "if this is not met, create that task". While a task works, your AI can start follow-up work when it judges the plan needs it, always tied to a goal on the quest (see Follow-up work stays on the plan under Autopilot).

To make the check meaningful, say what done looks like in your request: "done when the comparison lists three options with prices and a recommendation".

**Can I tell it to run task B after task A?** Not between tasks. Put both steps in one request, or build a Workflow whose steps start one after another.

**Follow-up work stays on the plan.** A task started from another task belongs to the same quest and the same goal as the task it came from. When an AI rep or Autopilot starts follow-up work, it says which goal that work serves: an existing goal, or a new sub-goal it creates under the goal it was working on, with an owner, a deadline and the outcome it moves. If a goal already stands for the work, it uses that goal instead of adding a duplicate. When the new goal belongs to a teammate, the task runs in that teammate's AI lane.

workflows_intro.title: Workflows: what they are and how to start one
workflows_intro.text:
# Workflows

A workflow shows who does what, and when, as a diagram: steps joined by arrows. Each step is run either by a person on your team or by one of your AI representatives, and each one says what needs to happen and by when. Quest watches whether it actually happened, so a missed step shows up as a risk instead of going unnoticed.

Workflows belong to a **team** or an **organization**, not to a single quest. One workflow can touch several quests, and a step can be tagged with the quest it belongs to. (A quest that has no team keeps its own workflows on the quest page; see [Workflows on a quest](#workflows-on-a-quest).)

## Why workflows exist

Without visible commitments, shared work drifts: everyone assumes someone else sent the update, and nobody notices the step that quietly never happened. A workflow writes the routine down as a diagram, gives every step one owner and a time, and then checks the clock against what was actually recorded. The point is not the picture. It is that a late or missed step shows up as a risk with a name on it while there is still time to nudge, reassign or fix it. And because a step can belong to one of your AI representatives, the routine part of the work (a Monday briefing, a reminder, a posted result) can run on its own, while the steps that need a person stay with a person.

## Who workflows suit

- **A team with a recurring routine**: a weekly review, a monthly report, a hand-off chain where one person's output is the next person's input.
- **A lead who needs to see whether the routine is happening**, without chasing people for updates.
- **A group that wants AI to do the routine steps** (brief the team, post the result) and people to do the judgment steps (reply, approve).
- **An organization with several teams**, which can see every team's workflows and their risks in one list.
